multiDecisionAssessment.rationale: The combined pathway scores tissue evaluation and then resection selection. Only the separately approved treatment-only and reverse-location management variants are active at Level 0.
Each approved patient arrives with an ultrasound report. Ordering ultrasound, an exact surveillance schedule, and later intervention would be separate concepts.

value.title: Select biliary decompression from the postoperative duct map
fairness: Single-best-answer concern: the findings support a communicating postoperative bile leak with maintained duct continuity, but do not clearly resolve plastic stenting versus sphincterotomy. Stenting is a plausible best choice; I cannot establish its exclusive superiority from the displayed leak characterization. This is a ranking uncertainty, not a claim that stenting is incorrect.

Importance: high; recognizing and managing a postoperative bile leak is practical general-surgery knowledge. Realism: hepatobiliary review is credible, but a patient bringing records while still eating and walking on the ward mixes clinic and inpatient viewpoints.

F02: the original remote-nerve distractors and supplied shoulder-referral mechanism are fully removed. The replacement tests bile-leak intervention instead of referred-pain anatomy; flag-specific wording is resolved by replacement, but the new item is not fully acceptable.

Review scope for this report: judgments use only each item's after Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task and Options; the standard and flag handoff supply the rubric and original concerns. Clinical rankings are offline reviewer judgments, not fresh source verification or Melissa Rowland's clinical approval. Difficulty is predicted, not measured.

Cue interpretation throughout: a necessary raw clinical discriminator is not automatically an unfair cue. Empty cues means no independently exploitable surface cue was identified; an item can still be too easy through classic recognition or weak competitors. Difficulty and fairness comments distinguish those problems. No runtime rendering, prior feedback, source ledger, timing metadata or hidden author rationale was used to adjudicate the displayed items.
suggestions: Have the clinician adjudicate ERCP stent versus sphincterotomy for this exact leak pattern. Either supply a supported patient-specific discriminator or replace the overlapping intervention with a credible but distinguishable plan.
Place the learner explicitly in the ongoing inpatient/hepatobiliary discussion; preserve the drainage response and duct-continuity observations.
Retain the useful two steps: interpret leak anatomy, then select the appropriate access/intervention.

value.title: Select leak diversion in a patient with a competing bleeding risk
fairness: The best offered intervention is plastic stenting: the resident must interpret a communicating stump leak with preserved main-duct continuity, then incorporate ongoing anticoagulation when comparing stenting with sphincterotomy. Covered metal stenting is a credible escalation error, although weaker than sphincterotomy here.

Importance: high, practical postoperative complication management. Realism: the current ward setting and concurrent pulmonary embolus are coherent. The heparin record is duplicated but is decision-critical clinical information, not a nonmedical answer match.

Owner flag F02: fully resolved at the wording level by replacement; the remote-nerve distractors and supplied referred-pain mechanism are absent. The replacement assesses bile-leak management, not the original anatomy objective.

Scope for this entire report: all 40 packet items are covered, including 38 revisions and the two frozen PASS items. Clinical judgments use only the after Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task and Options; titles are identifiers, not learner cues. The standard, owner-flag handoff and first review provide review context. No author self-check, rationale, earlier/future feedback or hidden eligibility field establishes a verdict. The B2B24 image referenced by Exhibit was inspected.

All clinical judgments are offline editorial assessments, not fresh source verification or Melissa Rowland's approval. Drafts remain needs_clinician_review. Difficulty is predicted for PGY-2/3, not measured. Necessary raw discriminators are not automatically unfair cues; an empty cues array does not imply that the item is difficult. Runtime waits, randomization, finite profiles and sequence leakage were outside this after-fields-only review.
suggestions: Preserve the duct-continuity and anticoagulation facts; the repeated heparin administration sentence can be consolidated without changing the decision.

value.title: Duct continuity before a minor-leak stent pathway
fairness: The learner must recognize the limits of the endoscopically filled tree, then choose an investigation that can address the separate branch and active biliary communication. A repeat injection and scintigraphic leak study are credible nearby errors with different limitations.

The image exists, is legible, and agrees with its description. 'Junction not resolved' and the unrepresented branch identify genuine limits of the studies rather than prove a disconnected duct; that distinction must remain.
Hepatobiliary-contrast MR cholangiography is a reasonable best offered next study. The current record does not prove a particular transection classification or make every repeat ERCP useless.

Importance: high for bile-duct injury/source mapping, with specialist-level test selection making this a defensible stretch item. Realism: a drained, persistent postoperative leak can undergo planned specialist assessment; clinical stability and contrast eligibility would be checked in actual care.
suggestions: Retain both study panels and the distinction between unseen anatomy and proven discontinuity.
Have the clinician verify the exact contrast-study indication and avoid feedback claiming the diagram proves duct transection. The present editorial PASS is not clinical sign-off.

value.title: Duct continuity before a minor-leak stent pathway
fairness: The image was inspected and is legible. Contrast confined to the main communicating tree does not settle the unrepresented branch, and the noncontrast map leaves its junction unresolved. The learner must infer the coverage limitation and select a complementary anatomic/functional study.

Hepatobiliary-contrast MR cholangiography is a defensible best offered study. Repeat retrograde injection may reproduce the same coverage limitation, while scintigraphy is less suited to the requested detailed anatomy. This ranking and feasibility merit hepatobiliary clinician review; no new source verification was performed.
The labels identifying an unrepresented branch and unresolved junction describe the study limitations needed for fairness; they do not name the required contrast-enhanced examination.

Importance: high for bile-duct injury recognition and referral; the precise imaging protocol is a stretch topic. Realism: ongoing drained bile with discrepant studies is plausible in a clinic-to-specialist pathway.
suggestions: Preserve the contrast distribution and unresolved branch, and ensure the clinical review confirms the intended next-study ranking. Do not present the schematic as a real patient image or imply that contrast excretion is guaranteed in every patient.

question.stem: Which endoscopic intervention should be planned for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Biliary plastic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: The anatomy supports internal diversion of a communicating minor leak. A stent can be inserted without dividing the papilla, avoiding the additional sphincterotomy bleeding exposure while anticoagulation remains necessary.

answerChoices.label: Biliary sphincterotomy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Papillary division can lower resistance but creates a higher-bleeding-risk intervention here. It is not interchangeable with stent diversion in this anticoagulated patient.

answerChoices.label: Covered biliary metal stenting
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Covered metal stents have a role in selected complex or refractory leaks. Ongoing output after external drainage does not by itself establish failure of initial plastic-stent diversion.

question.stem: What is the appropriate surgical implication of these fully confirmed T1a findings?

answerChoices.label: Completion liver and nodal resection is required
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The verified T1a depth and complete resection do not automatically require completion radical surgery.

answerChoices.label: Completion extrahepatic bile-duct excision is required
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This fully resected T1a profile does not establish routine duct removal.

answerChoices.label: Negative margins permit routine noncancer follow-up
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A sufficient resection does not make invasive cancer benign or eliminate specialist follow-up.

question.explanation: The correct answer is “Simple cholecystectomy may be sufficient.” The recommendation is narrowly tied to completely removed T1a disease. The verified T1a depth and complete resection do not automatically require completion radical surgery. This fully resected T1a profile does not establish routine duct removal. A sufficient resection does not make invasive cancer benign or eliminate specialist follow-up.

decisionNodes.stem: Which pathologic T category fits invasive gallbladder carcinoma confined to the lamina propria?
decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “T1a disease.” Lamina-propria invasion without muscular invasion defines T1a. In-situ disease does not invade the lamina propria. T1b requires muscular-layer invasion. T2 requires a deeper extent than the invasion described.

decisionNodes.stem: Which surgical plan fits completely resected margin-negative incidental T1a gallbladder cancer?

answerChoices.label: Accept the cholecystectomy with specialist follow-up
Return to routine follow-up without specialist review

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Accept the cholecystectomy with specialist follow-up.” These constrained findings do not automatically require radical re-resection. Confirmed completely resected margin-negative T1a disease does not automatically need radical re-resection. Routine bile-duct removal is not required by this completely resected T1a profile. Adequacy of the operation does not make invasive carcinoma benign or eliminate specialist follow-up.

question.stem: Which next investigation should guide {patientName}'s persistent postoperative drainage?
question.explanation: Do not equate a main-duct injection without visible escape with absence of every biliary source. The drainage and the nonrepresented segment create an anatomical question that the same downstream injection may not answer. Hepatobiliary-contrast MRCP can localize leakage and evaluate duct relationships before the team selects a minor-leak stent or a different HPB pathway. The schematic does not itself prove a particular repair or mandate an operation.

exhibit.description: Constructed two-panel duct record. The endoscopic injection fills the main channel to the duodenum and two central branches without visible escape. A branch in liver segment S is not included in that filled tree. The MR panel shows that branch approaching the drained collection; its junction with the central tree is unresolved.
exhibit.caption: Constructed duct-study observations; shaded channels contain injected contrast. Not a patient image.

answerChoices.label: Arrange hepatobiliary-contrast magnetic resonance cholangiography
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent bile plus a duct segment outside the filled endoscopic tree requires an anatomical study that can map upstream segments and localize excreted biliary contrast, rather than assume the filled main duct represents every source.

answerChoices.label: Arrange repeat endoscopic retrograde cholangiography contrast study
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating injection from the same downstream lumen can again fail to show a source outside the communicating filled tree.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating injection from the same downstream lumen can again fail to show a source outside the communicating filled tree.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next investigation should guide {patientName}'s persistent postoperative drainage?

answerChoices.label: Arrange hepatobiliary-contrast magnetic resonance cholangiography
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent bile plus a duct segment outside the filled endoscopic tree requires an anatomical study that can map upstream segments and localize excreted biliary contrast, rather than assume the filled main duct represents every source.

answerChoices.label: Arrange repeat endoscopic retrograde cholangiography contrast study
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating injection from the same downstream lumen can again fail to show a source outside the communicating filled tree.

answerChoices.label: Arrange hepatobiliary scintigraphy for leakage
answerChoices.rationale: This can demonstrate activity of a leak but provides less spatial information for the branch relationship needed before another intervention.

decisionNodes.explanation: Do not equate a main-duct injection without visible escape with absence of every biliary source. The drainage and the nonrepresented segment create an anatomical question that the same downstream injection may not answer. Hepatobiliary-contrast MRCP can localize leakage and evaluate duct relationships before the team selects a minor-leak stent or a different HPB pathway. The schematic does not itself prove a particular repair or mandate an operation.

A branch in liver segment S is not included in that filled tree. The MR panel shows that branch approaching the drained collection; its junction with the central tree is unresolved.

question.stem: Which procedure should be requested next for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic transpapillary plastic-stent placement
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent drainage with demonstrated major-duct continuity and a controlled cavity fits the minor-leak pathway. Transpapillary stenting addresses the ongoing leak rather than repeating collection drainage.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous exchange for a larger drainage catheter
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Catheter escalation is appropriate for an inadequately drained collection. Here the postdrainage CT shows a collapsed cavity; the continuing problem is leakage into it.

answerChoices.label: Operative reconstruction with a hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Reconstruction is a credible consideration after a major duct injury, but the demonstrated continuity and localized stump leak do not establish that indication.

question.explanation: The images show preserved major-duct continuity and a localized stump leak into an already drained cavity. Persistent minor leakage in this setting supports ERCP with transpapillary plastic-stent treatment. A larger drain would address residual collection, while reconstruction would address a different injury pattern. Sepsis, peritonitis or an uncontrolled collection would change the sequence.

question.stem: Which next plan should be arranged for {patientName}'s incidental gallbladder carcinoma?

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary surgical consultation
answerChoices.rationale: Muscular invasion is T1b and falls outside the completely removed T1a pathway; specialist reassessment is required.

answerChoices.label: Routine post-cholecystectomy surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A negative margin does not convert muscular invasion into lamina-propria-limited T1a disease.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A negative margin does not convert muscular invasion into lamina-propria-limited T1a disease.

answerChoices.label: Port-site scar excision
answerChoices.rationale: The documented depth requires specialist reassessment of the gallbladder primary; a port-site procedure does not resolve that planning question.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The documented depth requires specialist reassessment of the gallbladder primary; a port-site procedure does not resolve that planning question.

question.explanation: Gallbladder carcinoma invading muscle is T1b. Negative margins do not make the T1a simple-cholecystectomy rule applicable. This draft calls for HPB review and withholds a particular further operation pending targeted verification.

question.stem: Which postoperative cancer-planning sequence best fits {patientName}'s revised pathology?
question.explanation: First interpret the wall layer rather than the word superficial, then distinguish depth-driven reassessment from a duct-margin problem. This is T1b muscular invasion, so the completely resected T1a pathway cannot be applied. HPB assessment of completion surgery is the specific next planning issue; this draft does not prescribe an unverified hepatic or nodal extent.

answerChoices.label: HPB assessment of completion oncologic resection
answerChoices.rationale: Muscular invasion is outside the completely removed T1a observation pathway. The staging/fitness information makes assessment of completion oncologic surgery the remaining planning question; this is not an automatic operation.

answerChoices.label: HPB assessment of post-cholecystectomy surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A clear cystic-duct margin does not make smooth-muscle invasion equivalent to a completely resected lamina-propria-limited tumor.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A clear cystic-duct margin does not make smooth-muscle invasion equivalent to a completely resected lamina-propria-limited tumor.

answerChoices.label: HPB assessment of duct-stump re-excision
answerChoices.rationale: This directs the next workup to an involved duct margin, whereas the actual changed finding is depth in the gallbladder wall, with a clear duct margin.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This directs the next workup to an involved duct margin, whereas the actual changed finding is depth in the gallbladder wall, with a clear duct margin.

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old woman, returns after cholecystectomy. The original summary called the incidental carcinoma superficial. On specialist slide review, tumor nests are present within smooth-muscle bundles beneath the lamina propria; the cystic-duct margin is free of tumor. Staging CT shows no distant disease. She walks to the shops and climbs the stairs at home without cardiopulmonary symptoms.

question.stem: Which finding requires HPB reassessment before {patientName}'s proposed minor-leak stent pathway is accepted?

answerChoices.label: Interruption of the main bile-duct lumen
answerChoices.rationale: The preserved-continuity prerequisite is not present; the minor-leak rule does not establish a treatment plan for this injury.

answerChoices.label: Presence of a drained postoperative fluid collection
answerChoices.rationale: A drained collection does not itself invalidate an endoscopic pathway for a true minor leak with continuity.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A drained collection does not itself invalidate an endoscopic pathway for a true minor leak with continuity.

answerChoices.label: Biliary contrast visible outside the duct lumen
answerChoices.rationale: Extravasation establishes leakage but does not distinguish a continuity-preserved minor leak from the supplied discontinuity.

question.explanation: The recorded transpapillary-stent teaching is limited to a persistent minor leak with preserved common-duct continuity. Here the anatomical finding changes that premise. proposedNodes.objective: Select internal diversion for persistent communicating leakage after collection control.
proposedNodes.task: Which intervention should the hospital team have selected for {patientName} at this point?

choices.label: ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
choices.rationale: The main duct communicates with the duodenum and the collection is controlled. Internal diversion treats continuing leakage.

choices.label: Percutaneous exchange of the collection drain
choices.rationale: Continued bile can suggest catheter failure, but the cavity has contracted around the catheter.
choices.temptation: Attribute continued output to failed collection drainage.
choices.counterfactual: An enlarging collection with a displaced catheter would favor drainage revision.

choices.label: Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction
choices.rationale: The observed continuity and stump source do not establish a need for major reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Treat any bile leak as a main-duct transection.
choices.counterfactual: Separated main ducts would require specialist reconstruction planning.

proposedNodes.explanation: Persistent bile output must be interpreted with the duct map and the drained cavity. These observations support ERCP plastic-stent diversion for a communicating stump leak. They do not establish the indication for major duct reconstruction.
reasoningSteps: Infer a communicating side leak from main-duct passage with stump extravasation.
Combine that anatomy with a controlled cavity to choose internal diversion.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Mistake continued output for catheter failure or major duct disruption.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: Main-duct continuity and cavity contraction despite ongoing bile drainage.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: An enlarging pocket around a displaced catheter favors drainage revision; separated main ducts invalidate routine leak stenting.
proposedNodes.deletionTest: CT establishes collection control; duct passage distinguishes the reconstructive alternative. Earlier shoulder symptoms and exact volumes were deleted.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: Covered the key across complaint and presentation. Replaced the old task phrase persistent minor leak with preserved duct continuity with a neutral intervention task. All three labels name actual procedures; no sphincterotomy-versus-stent overlap is introduced.
manualAuthorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: One hospital intervention decision; three procedural plans.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Infer a communicating side leak from main-duct passage with stump extravasation. Then: Combine that anatomy with a controlled cavity to choose internal diversion.
manualAuthorGate.predictedDifficulty: Predicted moderate: continued output competes with evidence that the cavity is already controlled.
manualAuthorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: Stenting treats the demonstrated communicating leak after collection control. This does not rank every endoscopic technique for every leak.

proposedNodes.sequenceReview: First feedback does not reveal the later CT or subsequent procedure.

proposedNodes.objective: Choose intraductal sampling while preserving potential curative pathways.
proposedNodes.task: Which primary-lesion sampling plan should the HPB team choose for {patientName}?

choices.label: ERCP brushings with intraductal forceps biopsies
choices.rationale: Intraductal sampling can assess the hilar stricture without a transperitoneal primary-lesion needle track.

choices.label: EUS-guided needle biopsy of the hilar primary
choices.rationale: This can create a primary-lesion track outside the duct and risk compromising curative options.
choices.temptation: Generalize distal-stricture EUS sampling to a potentially curable hilar primary.
choices.counterfactual: An accessible metastatic node or extraluminal lesion in an inoperable case is a different EUS target.

choices.label: Percutaneous needle biopsy of the hilar primary
choices.rationale: A percutaneous primary track carries a similar dissemination concern in a potential curative pathway.
choices.temptation: Choose the most direct-looking primary biopsy route without considering future treatment.
choices.counterfactual: An intrahepatic tumor or distant metastasis after MDT review can appropriately undergo image-guided biopsy.

proposedNodes.explanation: The tissue target and intended treatment matter. A potentially curable perihilar primary should not automatically undergo transperitoneal needle biopsy. ERCP-based intraductal methods provide a supported alternative. This does not prohibit EUS sampling of every node or establish transplant eligibility.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish a hilar primary from distal duct or metastatic sampling targets.
Select a route that respects possible curative treatment constraints.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Apply a distal EUS-primary sampling rule to a potentially curable hilar lesion.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: Primary at the confluence with curative pathways still under evaluation.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: Accessible extraluminal metastatic disease or a clearly inoperable case changes the target and may support EUS tissue acquisition.
proposedNodes.deletionTest: Site and curative intent determine the needle-track boundary. No exact transplant size cutoff or assumed candidacy is introduced.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: The task asks about primary-lesion sampling rather than naming a safety hazard. All labels are specific tissue routes with wait metadata. Curative intent is necessary to rank them, not generic permission for a cautious answer.
manualAuthorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: One primary-lesion tissue-acquisition plan.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Distinguish a hilar primary from distal duct or metastatic sampling targets. Then: Select a route that respects possible curative treatment constraints.
manualAuthorGate.predictedDifficulty: Predicted hard: a generally useful biopsy technique becomes inappropriate because of site and downstream treatment.
manualAuthorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: Two guidelines support intraductal assessment and caution with potentially curable hilar primary needle sampling.

proposedNodes.sequenceReview: The first feedback explains sampling only; it does not name a future drainage side.

proposedNodes.objective: Select imaging that evaluates both collections and possible associated vascular injury.
proposedNodes.task: Which additional study should the hospital team have obtained for {patientName} at that stage?

choices.label: Multiphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT
choices.rationale: This evaluates collections, hepatic perfusion and vascular injury in the same postoperative assessment.

choices.label: Hepatobiliary-contrast MR cholangiography
choices.rationale: This adds duct and leak information but does not replace the initial vascular and collection assessment raised by the Doppler findings.
choices.temptation: Anchor on bile and obtain only detailed duct mapping.
choices.counterfactual: After vascular and collection assessment, an unresolved leak source or continuity question can favor this study.

choices.label: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy with delayed images
choices.rationale: This can show active leakage but provides less anatomical and vascular information for the present combined concern.
choices.temptation: Confirm leakage while failing to characterize the associated arterial concern.
choices.counterfactual: An unresolved active-leak question after structural mapping may justify scintigraphy.

proposedNodes.explanation: The missing decision information concerns more than bile leakage: the arterial finding and collection need structural assessment. Multiphasic CT evaluates those domains. Dedicated duct mapping remains a separate potential investigation, not a substitute for vascular assessment.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that uncertain arterial flow adds a vascular question to the postoperative bile problem.
Choose a study that assesses perfusion, vessels and collections rather than leak activity alone.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Anchor on the bile leak and overlook possible vasculobiliary injury.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: Unestablished right hepatic arterial flow in addition to a collection and duct dilation.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: If CT already assessed vessels and the only unresolved issue were leak localization, dedicated contrast MR cholangiography becomes appropriate.
proposedNodes.deletionTest: The Doppler finding changes the preferred modality; collection and stable historical status justify the current study-selection phase.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: No task repeats vascular, perfusion or multiphasic. All three are credible postoperative investigations and all have waits. The Doppler limitation is raw acquisition evidence rather than an author-supplied vascular diagnosis.
manualAuthorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: One additional imaging study.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Recognize that uncertain arterial flow adds a vascular question to the postoperative bile problem. Then: Choose a study that assesses perfusion, vessels and collections rather than leak activity alone.
manualAuthorGate.predictedDifficulty: Predicted moderate to hard: shift from the familiar leak-localization test to combined structural assessment.
manualAuthorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: WSES directly supports CT collection and vascular assessment; single adequate guideline for the exact ranking.

proposedNodes.sequenceReview: The first feedback does not teach what to do for a subsequently confirmed isolated artery interruption.

proposedNodes.objective: Choose expert rescue biliary drainage after failed endoscopic cannulation.
proposedNodes.currentUpdate: The next outside procedure report states that the ERCP team could not reach the papilla because of malignant duodenal narrowing. The stomach remains accessible and the left intrahepatic ducts are dilated. He has no hemodynamic instability. The referral center has teams experienced in both EUS-guided biliary drainage and percutaneous drainage.
proposedNodes.task: Which rescue drainage procedure should the referral team discuss for {patientName}?

choices.label: EUS-guided biliary drainage
choices.rationale: After failed ERCP, expert EUS-guided drainage is favored when anatomy and local experience support it.

choices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
choices.rationale: This is an important alternative, but current BSG guidance favors expert EUS drainage after failed distal-obstruction ERCP when feasible.
choices.temptation: Treat failed papillary access as requiring a percutaneous route in every patient.
choices.counterfactual: Unavailable EUS expertise or unsuitable EUS anatomy would favor percutaneous drainage.

choices.label: Operative bypass with hepaticojejunostomy
choices.rationale: A surgical bypass is more invasive than the expert rescue approaches available for this stable patient.
choices.temptation: Escalate from failed ERCP directly to an operation.
choices.counterfactual: Failure or infeasibility of less-invasive drainage could make bypass reasonable.

proposedNodes.explanation: Papillary access failed; repeating the same route is not the remaining decision. The accessible stomach and dilated ducts support considering EUS-guided drainage at an experienced center. Percutaneous drainage remains a valid alternative if EUS access or expertise is unsuitable. No exact drainage tract or stent specification is keyed.
reasoningSteps: Recognize access failure rather than failure of bile flow through a placed device.
Combine anatomy and specialist capability to choose a supported rescue route.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Assume every failed ERCP mandates percutaneous drainage or operative bypass.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: Failed papillary access with usable EUS access anatomy and experienced rescue teams.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: If EUS drainage is unavailable or anatomically unsuitable, percutaneous drainage becomes the favored offered route.
proposedNodes.deletionTest: Failed papillary access, reachable stomach and duct dilation establish rescue anatomy. Both teams are described to avoid hiding a resource constraint.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: The capability sentence is retained because guideline ranking depends on expertise; it names both competing services rather than uniquely permitting the key. Options compare actual rescue procedures. Corrected patient-sex consistency in the final author pass.
manualAuthorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: One rescue biliary drainage procedure.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Recognize access failure rather than failure of bile flow through a placed device. Then: Combine anatomy and specialist capability to choose a supported rescue route.
manualAuthorGate.predictedDifficulty: Predicted hard: separate route failure from device failure and apply the conditional EUS-versus-percutaneous ranking.
manualAuthorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: One adequate current guideline supports EUS rescue when feasible; exact patient suitability requires clinician review.

proposedNodes.sequenceReview: Failed papillary access and rescue anatomy are new. First feedback does not name EUS drainage.

proposedNodes.objective: Distinguish failed collection drainage from failed internal diversion after treatment.

exhibit.caption: Constructed hospital CT and procedure records
cells: One encapsulated subhepatic pocket; no free fluid elsewhere in the abdomen.
The pigtail lies anterior to the pocket.
An anterior percutaneous path enters the pocket without crossing bowel or pleura.
Stable blood pressure; tenderness remains confined to the right upper quadrant, without rigidity.

proposedNodes.task: Which initial procedure should the hospital team select to control {patientName}’s recurrent collection?

choices.label: Percutaneous image-guided catheter drainage
choices.rationale: The localized accessible pocket can be drained directly. The patient has neither diffuse contamination nor an absent access window requiring operative drainage.

choices.label: Laparoscopic washout with drain placement
choices.rationale: This is a real source-control alternative, but a contained pocket with a safe percutaneous route and stable physiology supports a less invasive initial approach.
choices.temptation: Treat postoperative infection as requiring abdominal washout regardless of its distribution.
choices.counterfactual: Diffuse peritoneal fluid, peritoneal signs or inability to obtain percutaneous control would favor operative source control.

choices.label: EUS-guided transluminal collection drainage
choices.rationale: Expert endoscopic collection drainage is possible in selected cases, but the available percutaneous route is the established initial approach for this postoperative biloma.
choices.temptation: Generalize successful internal biliary stenting to endoscopic drainage of the extrabiliary pocket.
choices.counterfactual: A selected inaccessible collection with a favorable gastrointestinal apposition at an expert center could prompt an EUS approach; evidence is limited.

proposedNodes.explanation: First identify a localized extrabiliary pocket, then assess the available drainage path and current physiology. Those findings favor percutaneous catheter drainage as the initial source-control procedure. Operative washout addresses diffuse or inadequately controlled contamination. Endoscopic biliary diversion and drainage of a collection are different procedures.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the stopped catheter and CT distribution as a contained undrained collection rather than diffuse contamination.
Use the safe access window and stable, localized examination to select the initial collection-drainage route.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Choose operative washout for every postoperative infected collection or conflate biliary stenting with collection drainage.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: Contained collection with a bowel-free percutaneous route and no diffuse peritoneal findings.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: Diffuse intraperitoneal fluid with rigidity, or failure of feasible catheter source control, shifts the initial plan toward operative washout.
proposedNodes.deletionTest: Catheter location remains visible. Distribution, access route and physiology now distinguish the closest operative alternative; the old sentence ruling out biliary-stent replacement was removed because device exchange is no longer an offered competitor.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: All options now control the collection. The key is not the only collection-directed label. Covered the key and compared catheter versus laparoscopic control from the actual access and distribution observations. Necessary warning signs were retained rather than obscured.
manualAuthorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: One initial source-control procedure; three named drainage approaches.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret the stopped catheter and CT distribution as a contained undrained collection rather than diffuse contamination. Then: Use the safe access window and stable, localized examination to select the initial collection-drainage route.
manualAuthorGate.predictedDifficulty: Fair moderate author prediction: localize the source, then decide whether imaging access and physiology support percutaneous or operative control. Advanced EUS is a secondary, explicitly limited alternative.
manualAuthorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: Percutaneous drainage is the best initial offered approach, supported by WSES and ESGE. No claim that EUS drainage is impossible or that surgery is never appropriate.

proposedNodes.sequenceReview: Standalone response candidate; earlier scored tasks and answer-specific feedback are not presented. Required history is stated in the case/exhibit.

proposedNodes.objective: Select interim proximal decompression when a septic obstructed duct cannot be reached from the papilla.

exhibit.caption: Constructed attributed outside-hospital studies
cells: The subhepatic cavity is collapsed around its catheter; no free intraperitoneal fluid.
Both hepatic duct systems are dilated. Excreted contrast exits the proximal common hepatic duct into the drained space and does not enter the downstream duct.
Contrast injected from the papilla fills the lower common duct to an abrupt clip-level end. The guidewire cannot pass that level.

proposedNodes.task: Which interim drainage procedure should the consulting HPB team arrange for {patientName} before definitive repair?

choices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
choices.rationale: The septic proximal ducts remain obstructed despite collection drainage, and the retrograde route cannot traverse the injury. Transhepatic drainage accesses the proximal system.

choices.label: ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
choices.rationale: This assumes an accessible path into the obstructed proximal ducts that the attributed injection and wire attempt did not establish.
choices.temptation: Apply the communicating minor-leak pathway to an unreachable proximal system.
choices.counterfactual: A communicating main duct with a cystic-stump side leak and effective collection control would favor transpapillary diversion.

choices.label: Percutaneous exchange of the collection catheter
choices.rationale: The collection is already collapsed; changing its catheter does not decompress the dilated proximal duct system.
choices.temptation: Treat every septic bile-leak patient by enlarging the collection drain.
choices.counterfactual: An enlarging pocket with a displaced or blocked collection catheter would instead favor collection-drain revision.

proposedNodes.explanation: The studies distinguish a controlled extrabiliary cavity from an obstructed proximal duct system. Infection persists while the papillary route cannot reach that system. Transhepatic biliary drainage is a supported interim decompression option under HPB management; no repair date or universal reconstruction is selected.
reasoningSteps: Use the two attributed duct studies to identify a proximal system not reached by the retrograde route.
Combine proximal obstruction and infection with a controlled collection to choose the compartment and access route for interim drainage.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Treat the collection or apply routine leak stenting when the proximal infected ducts remain inaccessible.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: Dilated proximal ducts plus failed retrograde passage, with the collection already collapsed.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: If the proximal ducts communicated with the papilla and a stump side leak persisted, a transpapillary stent would be appropriate; an enlarging collection would change the compartment requiring drainage.
proposedNodes.deletionTest: Removed the explicit “no continuous channel” interpretation. Shared HPB involvement retains the true expertise constraint without making transfer the unique answer. Each study has an acquisition/procedure attribution.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: All choices are interim drainage procedures under shared specialist care. Staffing cannot solve the options. Covered the key and re-solved the collection-versus-duct and proximal-access questions from the raw MR/ERCP findings.
manualAuthorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: One interim decompression procedure, with transfer, antibiotics and definitive repair outside the choice set.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Use the two attributed duct studies to identify a proximal system not reached by the retrograde route. Then: Combine proximal obstruction and infection with a controlled collection to choose the compartment and access route for interim drainage.
manualAuthorGate.predictedDifficulty: Predicted moderate to hard: continued infection despite a drained cavity can be mistaken for collection failure; two duct compartments and access directions must be interpreted.
manualAuthorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: WSES explicitly supports PTBD for septic complete obstruction when ERCP cannot restore drainage. Single-guideline, low-certainty support is recorded; the eighth postoperative day is a constructed chronology, not a new repair cutoff.

proposedNodes.sequenceReview: Standalone response candidate; earlier scored tasks and answer-specific feedback are not presented. Required history is stated in the case/exhibit.

proposedNodes.objective: Apply represented invasion depth and clear margins to avoid unnecessary completion surgery.

exhibit.caption: Constructed pathology and staging records
cells: The gallbladder and gross lesion are entirely submitted. Infiltrating malignant glands are present in the lamina propria.
Full-thickness sections beneath the lesion include muscle; no malignant glands are identified within or beyond it.
Free of carcinoma.
Free of carcinoma.
No residual mass or metastatic disease.

proposedNodes.task: Which next management plan best fits {patientName}’s completed resection and current records?

choices.label: Cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy
choices.rationale: The represented invasive carcinoma remains superficial to adequately sampled muscle, with complete removal and clear margins. Those findings do not establish a need for radical completion surgery.

choices.label: Completion liver-bed resection with portal lymphadenectomy
choices.rationale: This can address a deeper localized primary, but the adequately represented muscle and deeper wall here are uninvolved.
choices.temptation: Treat all invasive gallbladder cancers as requiring liver-bed and regional-node surgery.
choices.counterfactual: Perimuscular invasion in a fit patient with localized disease would favor this completion plan.

choices.label: Completion extrahepatic duct resection with reconstruction
choices.rationale: The specimen does not demonstrate residual carcinoma at the duct margin or adjacent duct wall.
choices.temptation: Treat a gallbladder primary as requiring duct excision despite complete shallow removal.
choices.counterfactual: Residual malignant involvement of the cystic-junction/common-duct wall would create a duct-clearance question.

proposedNodes.explanation: The tissue must be represented before its uninvolved status is applied. Here the gross lesion is submitted, muscle beneath it is present and uninvolved, the invasive glands remain in lamina propria, and margins are clear. That supports cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy rather than completion radical resection.
reasoningSteps: Interpret invasion depth from malignant glands relative to represented muscle, rather than equating “invasive” with deep wall disease.
Combine representative sampling, complete removal and clear margins to choose the postoperative management plan.

assignmentSummary.scopeIn: Bile-duct injury and postoperative leak, anatomy-directed repair/referral, congenital duct cysts, gallbladder neoplasia and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
assignmentSummary.scopeOut: Stone clearance and cholecystitis belong to gallbladder-duct-stones. Intrahepatic tumors belong to liver-malignancy.

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old woman, attends clinic with a drained collection after cholecystectomy. The drain continues to collect bile. CT has mapped the collection. The hospital's duct-injection study and noncontrast MR images are summarized in the constructed map; the procedure team is selecting the next anatomical study before another intervention.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next investigation should guide {patientName}'s persistent postoperative drainage?

answerChoices.label: Arrange hepatobiliary-contrast magnetic resonance cholangiography
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent bile plus a duct segment outside the filled endoscopic tree requires an anatomical study that can map upstream segments and localize excreted biliary contrast, rather than assume the filled main duct represents every source.

answerChoices.label: Arrange repeat endoscopic retrograde cholangiography contrast study
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating injection from the same downstream lumen can again fail to show a source outside the communicating filled tree.

answerChoices.label: Arrange hepatobiliary scintigraphy for leakage
answerChoices.rationale: This can demonstrate activity of a leak but provides less spatial information for the branch relationship needed before another intervention.

decisionNodes.explanation: Do not equate a main-duct injection without visible escape with absence of every biliary source. The drainage and the nonrepresented segment create an anatomical question that the same downstream injection may not answer. Hepatobiliary-contrast MRCP can localize leakage and evaluate duct relationships before the team selects a minor-leak stent or a different HPB pathway. The schematic does not itself prove a particular repair or mandate an operation.

exhibit.caption: Constructed duct-study observations; shaded channels contain injected contrast. Not a patient image.
exhibit.description: Constructed two-panel duct record. The endoscopic injection fills the main channel to the duodenum and two central branches without visible escape. A branch in liver segment S is not included in that filled tree. The MR panel shows that branch approaching the drained collection; its junction with the central tree is unresolved.

reviewDecisions.title: Persistent communicating leak after collection control
fairness: The best offered answer is ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting. The learner must distinguish a communicating stump leak from duct discontinuity, then integrate continuing output with a contracted, already drained cavity. Drain exchange and reconstruction represent different interpretations of those findings.
Duct continuity and collection control are necessary observations, not gratuitous answer labels. This is a high-yield postoperative bile-leak decision; difficulty is moderate rather than hard.
The first node is self-contained and does not require its later update. Its explanation does not disclose the later catheter displacement, although it primes the collection-versus-duct distinction.

Review scope: all 19 proposed nodes, comprising four rewrites and 15 new items, were assessed from candidate visible fields and preceding visible feedback. Seventeen kept records, 18 retirement proposals and five withheld teaching points were noted but not scored. No author self-check, key marker or post-answer explanation was treated as pre-answer evidence. This offline editorial review does not verify current guidelines or confer clinical approval. Runtime rendering, choice randomization and wait-preview behavior were not inspected. All drafts remain needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: For technical precision, identify the contrast-excreting MR examination as hepatobiliary-contrast MR cholangiography; ordinary MRCP does not itself show excreted contrast. The present description already supplies the necessary observed continuity and escape.

reviewDecisions.title: Recurrent collection after internal stenting

cues.phrase: the catheter pigtail lies anterior to the pocket
cues.why: Together with the visible pocket, this directly supplies the mechanical explanation and points to the only collection-directed option. It is valid clinical information, but the alternatives do not require a competing interpretation.

cues.phrase: the biliary stent draining into the duodenum without main-duct obstruction
cues.why: This explicitly neutralizes stent replacement; the preceding explanation has already said that the anatomy does not establish an indication for major reconstruction. Both distractors are therefore largely disposed of before this choice.

fairness: Image-guided drainage is the defensible best offered procedure for the newly undrained collection. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The later deterioration is coherent, and the update plus retained presentation provides enough information without remembering the first answer. However, knowing that an infected pocket needs drainage is essentially the only remaining inference; the stent and reconstruction distractors do not make it resident-level two-step reasoning.
Source control after a bile leak is high yield. Do not manufacture difficulty by removing infection findings or concealing catheter position.
suggestions: Rebuild the competition around two genuinely plausible source-control approaches, with observed collection accessibility, localization and patient condition determining the choice; retain resuscitation as shared care.
Alternatively request explicit acceptance as an easy source-control recognition item rather than presenting this exact version as a difficult resident question.

reviewDecisions.title: Referral after main-duct discontinuity
clarityIssues: The presentation calls these 'early studies' without identifying how the proximal and distal duct segments were demonstrated. A short attributed imaging report or constructed duct exhibit would make the anatomy easier to interpret.

cues.phrase: The initial hospital had no surgeon who performed complex biliary reconstruction.
cues.why: This makes transfer the obvious safe location answer against two explicitly local interventions. A reader need not interpret the duct map to reject local surgical repair.

cues.phrase: There was no continuous channel across the gap.
cues.why: The conclusion is stated after the already descriptive separate segments. Combined with the staffing sentence, the two intended inferences have largely been supplied.

fairness: HPB-center transfer with drainage maintained is the best offered plan. Avoiding a universal repair date or obligatory anastomosis is appropriate.

Major injury recognition and specialist referral are high yield, but this option set predominantly tests matching an unavailable local capability to transfer. The first node stands alone and the later peritonitis event is a coherent complication.
suggestions: Keep the genuine expertise constraint, but place specialist involvement in shared context and compare consequential interim care plans at the same stage.
Show the duct observations once, rather than adding an explicit discontinuity conclusion. Do not solve the difficulty problem by inventing a repair-time threshold or ranking disputed reconstructions.

reviewDecisions.title: Source control during diffuse biliary peritonitis

cues.phrase: a rigid, diffusely tender abdomen with falling blood pressure
cues.why: These essential emergency findings directly favor the only abdominal source-control operation. They should be preserved, but they make this a safety-recognition item with the present alternatives.

cues.phrase: the duct segments remain separated
cues.why: The prior node and its explanation already reject routine transpapillary stenting for this anatomy. Offering it again gives the learner a rehearsed elimination.

fairness: Urgent lavage and wide drainage is the best offered priority while resuscitation continues. Transhepatic diversion does not substitute for control of diffuse intraperitoneal contamination.

The new update changes the immediate priority coherently and is sufficient with the retained presentation. No confident clinical error is identified. The high-yield emergency is fair but easy, not two consequential independent reasoning steps.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as a safety/recognition exception, retaining the warning signs and current clinical priority.

If resident-level difficulty is required, construct a genuinely competing source-control decision from observed anatomy and physiology; replacing obvious alternatives or accepting an intentional easy item is preferable to obscuring the emergency.

reviewDecisions.title: Surgical disposition after purported T1a resection
clarityIssues: The entire candidate presentation is a 43-year-old woman attending clinic after cholecystectomy. Both currentUpdate and exhibit are null. The task asks about 'current pathology and staging findings', but none are supplied.
The handoff's claim that new report tables were verified cannot substitute for an actual visible exhibit; its after-version display also says 'Exhibit: none.'
'Which surgical plan' contrasts a nonsurgical follow-up option with two completion operations. A neutral next-management task would express the intended decision more accurately.

cues.phrase: Cancer-team follow-up after cholecystectomy
cues.why: This is the only follow-up choice among two completion resections. With the pathological discriminator missing, a learner can only guess from this category outlier, rather than interpret evidence.

fairness: There is no determinable best answer from the supplied candidate fields. Tumor diagnosis, depth, represented muscle, margin status, completeness of removal and staging results are all absent.

The explanation introduces 'margin-negative lamina-propria-limited disease' only after the answer. Neither that explanation, the identifier nor the key marker may retroactively supply missing evidence.
The explanation's general T1a management principle is plausible, but its application to this patient is unsupported. The missing baseline also compromises the later pathology-addendum sequence.

T1a versus deeper gallbladder invasion is high yield. Moderate is a provisional estimate of the intended depth-and-completeness decision, not a claim that the currently unanswerable item has legitimate difficulty.
suggestions: Restore a real candidate pathology/staging exhibit before this question, including independently worded observations of malignant invasion depth, represented uninvolved muscle and relevant margins/completeness.

Ensure the actual exported visible fields contain the report, then independently re-review both this node and its later addendum. Do not pass this node based on author validation claims or facts found only in feedback.

reviewDecisions.title: Changed depth on gallbladder pathology addendum
clarityIssues: 'Deeper levels from a retained block' and 'remains negative' refer to a baseline pathology report that is absent from the candidate first node.

'Glands among smooth-muscle bundles' does not explicitly identify malignant infiltrating glands. Benign epithelial invaginations can involve the muscle, so this abbreviated observation is not a secure standalone statement of carcinoma invasion.

cues.phrase: HPB assessment for completion oncologic resection
cues.why: This broad assessment is the only general escalation option; the alternatives are surveillance or assessment for a specific duct resection explicitly disfavored by the negative duct margin. It is also broader than, and potentially overlaps, assessment of extrahepatic duct resection.

cues.phrase: Completely removed, margin-negative lamina-propria-limited disease generally permits cancer-team follow-up after cholecystectomy.
cues.why: The preceding explanation teaches the depth-dependent follow-up rule. The later update supplies muscle involvement, leaving an obvious switch to the only broad escalation rather than a distinct difficult decision.

fairness: If the glands are confirmed invasive adenocarcinoma, renewed HPB assessment is a reasonable best next action. This does not establish that one definitive completion operation is mandatory for every T1b patient.
As written, the node depends on preceding feedback for a cancer baseline and does not fully stand alone. Its generic-versus-specific assessments are not cleanly mutually exclusive alternatives.

Depth-driven reassessment is high yield, but the current referral-versus-surveillance set is easy once the intended malignant diagnosis is assumed. No disputed T1b operation should be silently converted into a certain rule.
suggestions: Restore the earlier report and identify the new finding as malignant infiltrating glands, using reviewed pathological wording that distinguishes invasion from benign gland displacement/invagination.

Compare equally specific next actions at the same decision stage, and supply a meaningful remaining management discriminator. If evidence cannot support a closer procedural ranking, retain the clinical uncertainty and seek acceptance for a simpler reassessment objective.

reviewDecisions.title: Extent of completion surgery for perimuscular invasion

cues.phrase: Liver-bed resection with portal lymphadenectomy
cues.why: This key is assembled from majority option components: liver-bed resection occurs twice, portal lymphadenectomy occurs in all three, and omission of bile-duct resection occurs twice. It is also the shortest unextended operation. A component-convergence attack identifies it without interpreting tumor depth.

fairness: The best offered operation is liver-bed resection with portal lymphadenectomy. Depth supports completion oncologic surgery, while clear duct margins and absent liver/major vascular involvement limit the required extent. These are two consequential considerations and a high-yield distinction.

The presentation is sufficient for the offered comparison, and the explanation appropriately avoids claiming that major hepatectomy or routine duct resection is necessary. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.
The first node stands alone. Its explanation already teaches that duct extent follows margins, substantially scaffolding the next node.
suggestions: Rebuild the option set around independent credible planning errors rather than one core operation and two larger additions. Include an appropriate undertreatment competitor if it fits the tested stage, and check component convergence again.
Retain the necessary margin and invasion observations; do not remove them merely because they explain why a more extensive operation is unnecessary.

reviewDecisions.title: Additional resection for a positive duct-wall site
clarityIssues: The new positive frozen section follows an earlier negative cystic-duct margin. This can be coherent, but identify the newly sampled remaining duct/junction tissue so the resident can distinguish a different specimen from a contradictory reading of the same margin.

cues.phrase: The proximal bifurcation and intrapancreatic distal duct are uninvolved. The liver-bed margin is clear.
cues.why: The update excludes the regions addressed by the two much larger operations, leaving a direct match between involved common hepatic duct wall and the only isolated extrahepatic duct resection.

cues.phrase: its extent follows anatomy and margin requirements
cues.why: The preceding explanation states the exact principle this follow-up repeats. New positivity changes the answer, but the sequence reduces the task to applying the just-taught site-to-resection rule.

fairness: Extrahepatic bile-duct resection with hepaticojejunostomy is the best offered site-directed extension. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in that comparison.

The updated report plus retained presentation is sufficient, apart from specimen-orientation clarity. The alternatives address explicitly uninvolved anatomy, so this high-yield margin principle is easy rather than an independent two-step management problem.
suggestions: Identify the new specimen and relationship to the previous margin explicitly.

Use a distinct consequential clearance decision supported by a specimen map, or reduce the preceding answer-specific teaching. Compare clinically plausible extensions at the same site; do not conceal required proximal/distal boundaries to create artificial difficulty.

reviewDecisions.title: Treatment of a longstanding extrahepatic duct cyst

cues.phrase: fusiform enlargement of the extrahepatic duct
cues.why: Only 'Extrahepatic cyst excision and hepaticojejunostomy' repeats the named anatomical territory. The stem also says intrahepatic ducts are normal, making the left-hepatectomy alternative poorly competitive.

cues.phrase: no obstructing stone, stricture or solid nodule
cues.why: Together with the long extrahepatic distribution, this removes a plausible obstructive reason for the offered distal sphincterotomy. Both distractors target locations/problems not represented.

fairness: Extrahepatic cyst excision with reconstruction is the best offered treatment for the described congenital distribution. No confident clinical error is identified.

This standalone item supplies a recognizable type I pattern and asks for its customary operation. The two nominal steps are diagnosis recognition followed by associated-treatment recall, without a consequential competing patient factor.
Choledochal cyst classification and treatment are high yield. The longitudinal ultrasound can support congenital origin, but does not rescue the weak alternatives.
suggestions: Build a patient-specific anatomical or treatment-stage distinction that changes an otherwise plausible plan, using a clinician-supported comparison.
Replace the normal-left-liver resection foil with a credible same-stage error. Do not add disputed thresholds or a tenuous procedure comparison merely to make the item harder.

reviewDecisions.title: Initial tissue acquisition for a distal duct stricture

cues.phrase: EUS-guided sampling plus ERCP-based sampling
cues.why: The key combines both methods that appear separately as the other answers. It is the uniquely comprehensive 'both' response, allowing a test-wise choice without interpreting jaundice, location or pancreatic imaging.

cues.phrase: Cross-sectional staging has been completed before an endoscopic plan is chosen.
cues.why: This sentence supplies the workup sequence instead of testing it and does not discriminate among the three offered sampling plans.

fairness: Combined EUS- and ERCP-based tissue acquisition is a plausible preferred approach for this stated distal-stricture profile. No confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted; its exact guideline-specific preference was not independently verified offline.
The candidate is self-contained, but comparison of a combined plan against each component is not two consequential reasoning steps.

Biliary malignancy workup is important; this exact universal-looking combination preference is more specialized endoscopy guidance than a clearly top-priority general-surgery board distinction. The highYield rating is a qualitative scope judgment, not a measured exam-frequency claim.
The explanation establishes the initial sampling strategy but does not directly disclose the later cholangioscopy answer.
suggestions: Choose a concrete sampling target/route decision that depends on the observed anatomy, and compare equally complete plans rather than 'A plus B' versus A versus B.
Have the clinician verify the precise population and strength of the combined-sampling recommendation before scoring a categorical preference. Avoid expanding the item with decorative staging detail.

reviewDecisions.title: Persistent stricture after inadequate tissue sampling
clarityIssues: The update says EUS found no pancreatic or nodal target, but does not say that the duct narrowing itself was sampled. 'Repeat EUS needle sampling at the duct narrowing' therefore presupposes a prior procedure not established by the visible record.

cues.phrase: Repeat brush cytology of the same stricture
cues.why: Both distractors start with 'Repeat' and revisit the initial modalities, while cholangioscopy is the only novel technique. Novelty alone points toward the key after an update describing failed/inadequate initial sampling.

fairness: Persistent abnormal imaging plus inadequate samples supports further targeted acquisition; fibrosis in an inadequate specimen does not establish benign disease. Interpreting adequacy and then selecting a sampling approach can be a meaningful two-step, high-yield decision.

Cholangioscopy-guided biopsy is a defensible next approach. However, absence of a pancreatic or nodal target does not itself rule out EUS sampling of duct-wall thickening, and inadequate brushings do not make every improved repeat-sampling strategy wrong. The current record does not cleanly resolve the closest alternative.

The sequence follows the first node coherently. The later update contains the relevant prior methods and results, so it can stand without recalling the earlier selected option, once the EUS chronology is clarified.
suggestions: State what EUS actually visualized and sampled at the duct lesion, including any relevant technical limitation, without inventing a failed procedure.

Compare equally credible targeting strategies and specify what changes between attempts. Remove the unique-new-method versus two unchanged-repeat-method shortcut, while preserving the inadequate-sample observations.
Obtain clinician adjudication of the specific cholangioscopy-versus-repeat-EUS ranking for this distal lesion.

reviewDecisions.title: Primary-tumor sampling while transplant remains possible
fairness: ERCP brushings with intraductal forceps biopsies is the best offered primary-lesion sampling route. The resident must recognize the perihilar target, then consider the consequences of a transperitoneal primary-tumor needle route for a possible curative/transplant pathway.

The explicit primary-lesion target prevents inappropriate extrapolation from permitted nodal sampling. Transplant evaluation is a necessary constraint, not an unfair synonym for the answer. The ERCP-versus-two-needle-method pattern does not identify the preferred route without clinical knowledge.
This is a high-yield biopsy-route hazard. The explanation appropriately distinguishes primary sampling from sampling every node and does not claim actual transplant eligibility.

The first node stands alone. Later confirmed malignancy and selection of resection can follow evaluation of several curative options; the earlier explanation does not reveal the later drainage territory.

reviewDecisions.title: Initial drainage territory before right hepatectomy

cues.phrase: leaving the left liver
cues.why: The author explicitly computes the future remnant immediately before a left-versus-right-versus-both choice. It duplicates the inference from the planned right hepatectomy and favors the exact left-system label.

fairness: Given an already selected preoperative drainage strategy and no infected competing territory, targeting the left future remnant is the defensible best offered initial territory. No confident clinical error is identified.
The update is coherent after diagnosis and provides the resection plan independently of the first answer. Keeping the decision to drain in shared context appropriately narrows the task.

Future-remnant drainage is high yield, but the current item supplies the remnant and asks for one associated territory. Removing the explicit left-liver phrase alone would still leave mostly a single-rule application.
suggestions: Remove the redundant computed remnant, then add a clinically supported, consequential territory-selection problem that requires interpretation of a duct/drainage map and current findings.
Keep infection and planned-resection information needed for fairness; do not create difficulty by hiding whether another territory needs source control.

reviewDecisions.title: Endoscopic treatment of a traversable postoperative stricture

cues.phrase: The HPB team attributes it to the prior operation and is selecting an endoscopic treatment course.
cues.why: Both the benign postoperative interpretation and treatment modality have been selected for the learner, leaving a familiar device rule rather than the proposed anatomy-to-treatment reasoning.

cues.phrase: Temporary multiple plastic biliary stents
cues.why: The key is framed as temporary against explicitly 'Permanent' metal stenting and a sphincterotomy 'without stricture stenting'. Duration and omission wording make the alternatives look deliberately unsafe or incomplete.

cues.phrase: Papillary sphincterotomy without stricture stenting
cues.why: The label advertises failure to treat the named stricture rather than simply naming a plausible competing plan.

fairness: Temporary multiple plastic stents is the best offered course for the accepted benign traversable stricture. The explanation correctly limits the comparison and acknowledges removable covered metal stents as another strategy rather than claiming plastic superiority over every device.
Benign-stricture stent selection is high yield, but this is easy single-rule recall after the team has already supplied diagnosis and modality. The first node stands alone.

Scar without atypia and absence of a mass do not, by themselves, definitively exclude malignancy; the explicit HPB attribution permits this treatment question, but feedback should not teach those tests as universally conclusive.
suggestions: Use neutral procedure labels and replace the deliberately incomplete papillary option with a real clinical competitor.

Choose a supported patient/anatomical factor that changes a plausible endoscopic strategy, or retain this as an explicitly accepted basic device-safety item. Do not rank plastic against covered metal stenting without a defensible patient-specific reason.

MRCP shows a short smooth mid-duct narrowing with a continuous lumen and upstream dilation. questions.stem: Which intervention should the hospital team have selected for {patientName} at this point?

answerChoices.label: ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: The main duct communicates with the duodenum and the collection is controlled. Internal diversion treats continuing leakage.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous exchange of the collection drain
answerChoices.rationale: Continued bile can suggest catheter failure, but the cavity has contracted around the catheter.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Continued bile can suggest catheter failure, but the cavity has contracted around the catheter.

answerChoices.label: Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The observed continuity and stump source do not establish a need for major reconstruction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The observed continuity and stump source do not establish a need for major reconstruction.

questions.explanation: Persistent bile output must be interpreted with the duct map and the drained cavity. These observations support ERCP plastic-stent diversion for a communicating stump leak. They do not establish the indication for major duct reconstruction.

questions.stem: Which additional procedure should the hospital team prioritize for {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Image-guided drainage of the recurrent collection
answerChoices.rationale: The new pocket is not entered by the collection catheter; it requires source control.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with replacement of the biliary stent
answerChoices.rationale: The record shows internal drainage into the duodenum, while the collection catheter no longer enters the pocket.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The record shows internal drainage into the duodenum, while the collection catheter no longer enters the pocket.

answerChoices.label: Operative reconstruction of the common hepatic duct
answerChoices.rationale: The changed local problem is a separate fluid pocket, not evidence of main-duct disruption.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The changed local problem is a separate fluid pocket, not evidence of main-duct disruption.

questions.explanation: A functioning internal stent does not drain an extrabiliary collection. CT now demonstrates a pocket that the catheter no longer enters, making targeted collection drainage the immediate additional procedure. Resuscitation and infection treatment continue at the hospital.

questions.stem: Which biliary plan should the referring hospital have arranged for {patientName} after these studies?

answerChoices.label: HPB-center transfer with drainage maintained
answerChoices.rationale: The separated main ducts lie outside the routine communicating-leak stent pathway; drainage is maintained while specialist treatment is planned.

answerChoices.label: Local ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: A routine papillary stent cannot be assumed to bridge the observed gap.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A routine papillary stent cannot be assumed to bridge the observed gap.

answerChoices.label: Local duct-to-duct surgical anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: A local repair can compound a complex injury when reconstructive expertise is absent.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided sampling plus ERCP-based sampling

answerChoices.label: ERCP brush cytology as the sampling method
answerChoices.rationale: Brushing accesses the stricture but omits complementary tissue assessment and can be nondiagnostic.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided sampling as the sampling method
answerChoices.rationale: EUS is useful, but this jaundiced distal-duct profile supports complementary duct-based acquisition.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional endoscopic sampling approach should the HPB team select for {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Cholangioscopy-guided biopsy of the stricture

answerChoices.label: Repeat brush cytology of the same stricture

answerChoices.label: Repeat EUS needle sampling at the duct narrowing
answerChoices.rationale: The current study found no discrete extraluminal target; a complementary intraductal approach addresses the demonstrated sampling limitation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial drainage territory should the HPB team choose for {patientName}?

answerChoices.rationale: The left liver is the future remnant, so its drainage is the initial preoperative target.

answerChoices.rationale: Bilateral dilation does not itself establish a need to drain both; further territories depend on response or infection.

decisionNodes.stem: Which endoscopic course should the HPB team discuss for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Temporary multiple plastic biliary stents
answerChoices.rationale: A traversable benign postoperative stricture can be treated with a temporary stent course.

answerChoices.label: Permanent uncovered metal biliary stenting
answerChoices.rationale: An uncovered permanent device is unsuitable as a routine benign-stricture strategy because later removal is problematic.

answerChoices.label: Papillary sphincterotomy without stricture stenting
answerChoices.rationale: Papillary division does not provide prolonged treatment across the demonstrated mid-duct scar.

decisionNodes.explanation: The lesion is a traversable mid-duct scar, not a malignant obstruction or isolated papillary problem. Temporary stenting is a supported endoscopic strategy. A removable covered metal stent is another supported strategy not offered here; no superiority of plastic over every covered device is claimed.
sourceLabels: Endoscopic biliary stenting: indications, choice of stents, and results

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Years later, the outside record documents recurrent febrile jaundice. MRCP now shows a long high-duct scar ending below the hepatic confluence. At two expert ERCP attempts a guidewire could not cross it. A transhepatic drain relieved the infection. He has recovered, has no hepatic atrophy or metastases, and remains active.
decisionNodes.stem: Which definitive treatment should the HPB team evaluate for {patientName} after infection control?

answerChoices.label: Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: A clinically significant major stricture with recurrent infection and failed restoration of endoscopic drainage warrants reconstructive evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Another transpapillary plastic-stent course
answerChoices.rationale: This assumes passage across a scar that expert attempts could not traverse.

answerChoices.label: Permanent external transhepatic drainage
answerChoices.rationale: External drainage controls infection, but in this recovered fit patient it does not address the underlying scar as a durable reconstructive option.

decisionNodes.explanation: Temporary drainage has controlled the acute infection. The remaining problem is a major recurrent stricture that could not be traversed endoscopically. Specialist biliary reconstruction evaluation is appropriate; the date, access method and anastomotic details are not prescribed.
