decisionNodes.stem: Which additional study should the hospital team have obtained for {patientName} at that stage?

answerChoices.label: Multiphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT
answerChoices.rationale: This evaluates collections, hepatic perfusion and vascular injury in the same postoperative assessment.

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary-contrast MR cholangiography
answerChoices.rationale: This adds duct and leak information but does not replace the initial vascular and collection assessment raised by the Doppler findings.

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy with delayed images
answerChoices.rationale: This can show active leakage but provides less anatomical and vascular information for the present combined concern.

decisionNodes.explanation: The missing decision information concerns more than bile leakage: the arterial finding and collection need structural assessment. Multiphasic CT evaluates those domains. Dedicated duct mapping remains a separate potential investigation, not a substitute for vascular assessment.
sourceLabels: 2020 WSES guidelines for the detection and management of bile duct injury during cholecystectomy

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The outside multiphasic CT shows occlusion of the right hepatic artery, a patent right portal branch, and enhancement throughout the right liver without necrotic areas. The collection is drained, and she remains stable. The HPB team is planning staged biliary treatment.
decisionNodes.stem: Which vascular-liver plan should the HPB team have selected for {patientName} from this record?

answerChoices.label: Monitor hepatic perfusion during staged biliary care
answerChoices.rationale: Preserved portal flow and maintained parenchymal enhancement do not establish a need for emergency arterial reconstruction or liver removal.

answerChoices.label: Attempt immediate right hepatic arterial reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Arterial occlusion may prompt repair, but routine immediate reconstruction is not established for this stable, perfused liver.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with right hepatectomy during duct repair
answerChoices.rationale: There is no demonstrated right-liver necrosis or nonviable territory requiring resection.

decisionNodes.explanation: Arterial interruption and nonviable liver are different findings. Preserved portal flow and right-liver enhancement support specialist perfusion surveillance during biliary management rather than automatic arterial reconstruction or hepatectomy. This low-certainty boundary requires HPB clinician review.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial drainage plan should the HPB team discuss for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: ERCP with a covered self-expanding metal stent
answerChoices.rationale: Confirmed unresectable distal malignant obstruction supports a metal stent for durable palliation.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with serial plastic biliary stent exchanges
answerChoices.rationale: Plastic stenting can temporarily decompress the duct but is less suitable as the planned long-term palliative course.

answerChoices.label: Operative biliary bypass with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: Bypass may be needed in selected failed less-invasive pathways, but is not the preferred initial drainage route in this accessible distal obstruction.

decisionNodes.explanation: The metastatic confirmation changes the goal from curative resection to durable symptom-relieving drainage. For distal malignant obstruction, metal stenting is favored over a repeated plastic-stent course. The item does not score chemotherapy choice or expected survival.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The next outside procedure report states that the ERCP team could not reach the papilla because of malignant duodenal narrowing. The stomach remains accessible and the left intrahepatic ducts are dilated. He has no hemodynamic instability. The referral center has teams experienced in both EUS-guided biliary drainage and percutaneous drainage.
decisionNodes.stem: Which rescue drainage procedure should the referral team discuss for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: After failed ERCP, expert EUS-guided drainage is favored when anatomy and local experience support it.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: This is an important alternative, but current BSG guidance favors expert EUS drainage after failed distal-obstruction ERCP when feasible.

answerChoices.label: Operative bypass with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: A surgical bypass is more invasive than the expert rescue approaches available for this stable patient.

decisionNodes.explanation: Papillary access failed; repeating the same route is not the remaining decision. The accessible stomach and dilated ducts support considering EUS-guided drainage at an experienced center. Percutaneous drainage remains a valid alternative if EUS access or expertise is unsuitable. No exact drainage tract or stent specification is keyed.

reviewDecision.title: Persistent communicating leak after collection control
fairness: The best offered answer is ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting. The learner must distinguish a communicating stump leak from duct discontinuity, then integrate continuing output with a contracted, already drained cavity. Drain exchange and reconstruction represent different interpretations of those findings.
Duct continuity and collection control are necessary observations, not gratuitous answer labels. This is a high-yield postoperative bile-leak decision; difficulty is moderate rather than hard.
The first node is self-contained and does not require its later update. Its explanation does not disclose the later catheter displacement, although it primes the collection-versus-duct distinction.

Review scope: all 19 proposed nodes, comprising four rewrites and 15 new items, were assessed from candidate visible fields and preceding visible feedback. Seventeen kept records, 18 retirement proposals and five withheld teaching points were noted but not scored. No author self-check, key marker or post-answer explanation was treated as pre-answer evidence. This offline editorial review does not verify current guidelines or confer clinical approval. Runtime rendering, choice randomization and wait-preview behavior were not inspected. All drafts remain needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: For technical precision, identify the contrast-excreting MR examination as hepatobiliary-contrast MR cholangiography; ordinary MRCP does not itself show excreted contrast. The present description already supplies the necessary observed continuity and escape.

reviewDecision.title: Primary-tumor sampling while transplant remains possible
fairness: ERCP brushings with intraductal forceps biopsies is the best offered primary-lesion sampling route. The resident must recognize the perihilar target, then consider the consequences of a transperitoneal primary-tumor needle route for a possible curative/transplant pathway.

The explicit primary-lesion target prevents inappropriate extrapolation from permitted nodal sampling. Transplant evaluation is a necessary constraint, not an unfair synonym for the answer. The ERCP-versus-two-needle-method pattern does not identify the preferred route without clinical knowledge.
This is a high-yield biopsy-route hazard. The explanation appropriately distinguishes primary sampling from sampling every node and does not claim actual transplant eligibility.

The first node stands alone. Later confirmed malignancy and selection of resection can follow evaluation of several curative options; the earlier explanation does not reveal the later drainage territory.

reviewDecision.title: Imaging a possible combined vascular and biliary injury
fairness: Multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT is the best offered next study when both a collection and unresolved hepatic arterial flow require assessment. The learner must distinguish an unestablished arterial signal from a proven occlusion, then select imaging that addresses the broader structural question rather than only bile leakage.

The stability statement provides a legitimate timing boundary. Neither 'hepatic' nor 'contrast' uniquely identifies the key, and the imaging labels are parallel. MR cholangiography and scintigraphy are plausible bile-focused errors.
Recognizing associated vascular injury during bile-duct-injury evaluation is high yield. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in the offered modality comparison.
The first node stands alone; its explanation does not disclose whether a subsequently documented arterial occlusion warrants repair or resection.

answerChoices.rationale: This adds duct and leak information but does not replace the initial vascular and collection assessment raised by the Doppler findings.

reviewDecision.title: Rescue drainage after inaccessible papilla
fairness: EUS-guided drainage is a defensible best offered rescue approach at an experienced center after ERCP access failure in malignant distal obstruction. The learner must recognize that the failed route is papillary access, then integrate accessible stomach, dilated left ducts, stability and expertise when comparing alternative routes.

Percutaneous drainage remains a credible alternative, not an intrinsically wrong procedure. The explicit availability of expertise in both routes avoids making capability alone uniquely select EUS. The wording and explanation should preserve this preferred-versus-only-possible distinction.

The exact contemporary recommendation favoring EUS over percutaneous rescue was not independently source-verified in this offline review; no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The existing exact-version claim and clinician review remain necessary before clinical approval.

Rescue drainage after failed ERCP is a useful high-yield management sequence, though the advanced endoscopic details are less foundational than initial decompression. Difficulty is moderate, not hard.

The update coherently follows attempted ERCP and contains the cause of failure. With the retained presentation, it stands without remembering the earlier selected stent; the preceding explanation does not disclose this rescue answer.
suggestions: A lead-in asking for the preferred initial rescue approach would express the ranking more precisely than simply asking which procedure to 'discuss'. Keep percutaneous drainage acknowledged as a valid fallback.

questions.stem: Which intervention should the hospital team have selected for {patientName} at this point?

answerChoices.label: ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: The main duct communicates with the duodenum and the collection is controlled. Internal diversion treats continuing leakage.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous exchange of the collection drain
answerChoices.rationale: Continued bile can suggest catheter failure, but the cavity has contracted around the catheter.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Continued bile can suggest catheter failure, but the cavity has contracted around the catheter.

answerChoices.label: Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The observed continuity and stump source do not establish a need for major reconstruction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The observed continuity and stump source do not establish a need for major reconstruction.

questions.explanation: Persistent bile output must be interpreted with the duct map and the drained cavity. These observations support ERCP plastic-stent diversion for a communicating stump leak. They do not establish the indication for major duct reconstruction.

questions.stem: Which primary-lesion sampling plan should the HPB team choose for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: ERCP brushings with intraductal forceps biopsies
answerChoices.rationale: Intraductal sampling can assess the hilar stricture without a transperitoneal primary-lesion needle track.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided needle biopsy of the hilar primary
answerChoices.rationale: This can create a primary-lesion track outside the duct and risk compromising curative options.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This can create a primary-lesion track outside the duct and risk compromising curative options.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous needle biopsy of the hilar primary
answerChoices.rationale: A percutaneous primary track carries a similar dissemination concern in a potential curative pathway.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A percutaneous primary track carries a similar dissemination concern in a potential curative pathway.

questions.explanation: The tissue target and intended treatment matter. A potentially curable perihilar primary should not automatically undergo transperitoneal needle biopsy. ERCP-based intraductal methods provide a supported alternative. This does not prohibit EUS sampling of every node or establish transplant eligibility.

questions.stem: Which additional study should the hospital team have obtained for {patientName} at that stage?

answerChoices.label: Multiphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT
answerChoices.rationale: This evaluates collections, hepatic perfusion and vascular injury in the same postoperative assessment.

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary-contrast MR cholangiography
answerChoices.rationale: This adds duct and leak information but does not replace the initial vascular and collection assessment raised by the Doppler findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This adds duct and leak information but does not replace the initial vascular and collection assessment raised by the Doppler findings.

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy with delayed images
answerChoices.rationale: This can show active leakage but provides less anatomical and vascular information for the present combined concern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This can show active leakage but provides less anatomical and vascular information for the present combined concern.

questions.explanation: The missing decision information concerns more than bile leakage: the arterial finding and collection need structural assessment. Multiphasic CT evaluates those domains. Dedicated duct mapping remains a separate potential investigation, not a substitute for vascular assessment.

questions.stem: Which rescue drainage procedure should the referral team discuss for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: After failed ERCP, expert EUS-guided drainage is favored when anatomy and local experience support it.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: This is an important alternative, but current BSG guidance favors expert EUS drainage after failed distal-obstruction ERCP when feasible.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is an important alternative, but current BSG guidance favors expert EUS drainage after failed distal-obstruction ERCP when feasible.

answerChoices.label: Operative bypass with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: A surgical bypass is more invasive than the expert rescue approaches available for this stable patient.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A surgical bypass is more invasive than the expert rescue approaches available for this stable patient.

questions.explanation: Papillary access failed; repeating the same route is not the remaining decision. The accessible stomach and dilated ducts support considering EUS-guided drainage at an experienced center. Percutaneous drainage remains a valid alternative if EUS access or expertise is unsuitable. No exact drainage tract or stent specification is keyed.

questions.stem: Which initial procedure should the hospital team select to control {patientName}’s recurrent collection?

exhibit.caption: Constructed hospital CT and procedure records
cells: One encapsulated subhepatic pocket; no free fluid elsewhere in the abdomen.
The pigtail lies anterior to the pocket.
An anterior percutaneous path enters the pocket without crossing bowel or pleura.
Stable blood pressure; tenderness remains confined to the right upper quadrant, without rigidity.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous image-guided catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The localized accessible pocket can be drained directly. The patient has neither diffuse contamination nor an absent access window requiring operative drainage.

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic washout with drain placement
answerChoices.rationale: This is a real source-control alternative, but a contained pocket with a safe percutaneous route and stable physiology supports a less invasive initial approach.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a real source-control alternative, but a contained pocket with a safe percutaneous route and stable physiology supports a less invasive initial approach.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided transluminal collection drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Expert endoscopic collection drainage is possible in selected cases, but the available percutaneous route is the established initial approach for this postoperative biloma.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Expert endoscopic collection drainage is possible in selected cases, but the available percutaneous route is the established initial approach for this postoperative biloma.

questions.explanation: First identify a localized extrabiliary pocket, then assess the available drainage path and current physiology. Those findings favor percutaneous catheter drainage as the initial source-control procedure. Operative washout addresses diffuse or inadequately controlled contamination. Endoscopic biliary diversion and drainage of a collection are different procedures.

questions.stem: Which interim drainage procedure should the consulting HPB team arrange for {patientName} before definitive repair?

exhibit.caption: Constructed attributed outside-hospital studies
cells: The subhepatic cavity is collapsed around its catheter; no free intraperitoneal fluid.
Both hepatic duct systems are dilated. Excreted contrast exits the proximal common hepatic duct into the drained space and does not enter the downstream duct.
Contrast injected from the papilla fills the lower common duct to an abrupt clip-level end. The guidewire cannot pass that level.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The septic proximal ducts remain obstructed despite collection drainage, and the retrograde route cannot traverse the injury. Transhepatic drainage accesses the proximal system.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: This assumes an accessible path into the obstructed proximal ducts that the attributed injection and wire attempt did not establish.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This assumes an accessible path into the obstructed proximal ducts that the attributed injection and wire attempt did not establish.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous exchange of the collection catheter
answerChoices.rationale: The collection is already collapsed; changing its catheter does not decompress the dilated proximal duct system.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The collection is already collapsed; changing its catheter does not decompress the dilated proximal duct system.

questions.explanation: The studies distinguish a controlled extrabiliary cavity from an obstructed proximal duct system. Infection persists while the papillary route cannot reach that system. Transhepatic biliary drainage is a supported interim decompression option under HPB management; no repair date or universal reconstruction is selected.

questions.stem: Which next management plan best fits {patientName}’s completed resection and current records?

exhibit.caption: Constructed pathology and staging records
cells: The gallbladder and gross lesion are entirely submitted. Infiltrating malignant glands are present in the lamina propria.
Full-thickness sections beneath the lesion include muscle; no malignant glands are identified within or beyond it.
Free of carcinoma.
Free of carcinoma.
No residual mass or metastatic disease.

answerChoices.label: Cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented invasive carcinoma remains superficial to adequately sampled muscle, with complete removal and clear margins. Those findings do not establish a need for radical completion surgery.

answerChoices.label: Completion liver-bed resection with portal lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: This can address a deeper localized primary, but the adequately represented muscle and deeper wall here are uninvolved.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This can address a deeper localized primary, but the adequately represented muscle and deeper wall here are uninvolved.

answerChoices.label: Completion extrahepatic duct resection with reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The specimen does not demonstrate residual carcinoma at the duct margin or adjacent duct wall.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The specimen does not demonstrate residual carcinoma at the duct margin or adjacent duct wall.

questions.explanation: The tissue must be represented before its uninvolved status is applied. Here the gross lesion is submitted, muscle beneath it is present and uninvolved, the invasive glands remain in lamina propria, and margins are clear. That supports cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy rather than completion radical resection.

questions.stem: Which next oncologic management plan should the HPB team discuss for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Completion liver-bed resection with regional lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Perimuscular invasion supports completion oncologic surgery despite no visible residual mass; the clear duct margin does not create an indication for duct removal.

answerChoices.label: Cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A clear margin and negative CT do not make perimuscular invasion equivalent to completely removed lamina-propria-limited disease.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A clear margin and negative CT do not make perimuscular invasion equivalent to completely removed lamina-propria-limited disease.

answerChoices.label: Completion extrahepatic duct resection with reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: This directs resection to an uninvolved duct rather than the gallbladder bed and regional nodes.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This directs resection to an uninvolved duct rather than the gallbladder bed and regional nodes.

questions.explanation: A negative staging scan does not erase the microscopic depth of invasion. For this fit patient with localized perimuscular disease, completion liver-bed and regional nodal surgery is supported. The current record does not identify residual extrahepatic duct disease.

questions.stem: Which additional clearance procedure should the HPB team discuss for {patientName} from this specimen map?

exhibit.caption: Constructed specimen map from the completion operation
cells: Remaining cystic-duct stump, submitted along its length
No carcinoma identified.
Common hepatic duct wall at the cystic-duct junction, separately oriented
Infiltrating adenocarcinoma is present within this wall.
Liver-bed resection margin
No carcinoma identified.
Proposed proximal and distal duct-division edges, sampled separately
No carcinoma identified.

answerChoices.label: Segmental extrahepatic duct resection with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The malignant focus is in remaining common-duct wall beyond the tumor-free cystic stump. Duct excision with reconstruction addresses that site between clear sampled division edges.

answerChoices.label: Further excision of the remaining cystic-duct stump
answerChoices.rationale: This does not remove the separately represented malignant common hepatic duct wall; the stump itself is negative.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This does not remove the separately represented malignant common hepatic duct wall; the stump itself is negative.

answerChoices.label: Further resection of the gallbladder liver bed
answerChoices.rationale: This targets the wrong remaining specimen: the liver-bed margin is clear, while another oriented wall specimen contains tumor.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This targets the wrong remaining specimen: the liver-bed margin is clear, while another oriented wall specimen contains tumor.

questions.explanation: A negative cut edge on the removed gallbladder is not the same specimen as the remaining common hepatic duct wall sampled at completion surgery. The new map places carcinoma beyond the negative cystic stump, in a duct-wall segment bounded by clear sampled division edges. The offered clearance procedure must remove that segment rather than repeat excision of negative stump or liver-bed tissue.

questions.stem: Which long-term biliary plan should the HPB team discuss with {patientName} after recovery?

exhibit.caption: Constructed childhood operation and current duct records
cells: The enlarged duct was opened into the duodenum; the operative record states that no cyst wall was removed.
Fusiform common-duct enlargement remains from below the hepatic confluence to the intrapancreatic duct. No mural nodule is described.
The opening is patent, with no filling defect or anastomotic narrowing.

answerChoices.label: Completion cyst excision with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The old operation drained the cyst rather than removing it. A patent opening and symptom improvement do not remove the retained abnormal duct epithelium.

answerChoices.label: Surveillance after the previous cyst operation
answerChoices.rationale: The label previous surgery does not establish excision; the record and MRCP show retained cyst tissue that still needs definitive-treatment assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The label previous surgery does not establish excision; the record and MRCP show retained cyst tissue that still needs definitive-treatment assessment.

answerChoices.label: Revision of the cyst-duodenal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: A drainage revision may address a narrowed opening but leaves cyst epithelium in place; the current opening is patent.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A drainage revision may address a narrowed opening but leaves cyst epithelium in place; the current opening is patent.

questions.explanation: Interpret what the childhood operation actually removed. It created drainage but left the cyst wall, and MRCP confirms that the abnormal duct remains. Relief of obstruction is therefore not equivalent to definitive cyst treatment. Completion excision and reconstruction warrants HPB discussion after recovery, with exact operative extent and later surveillance individualized.

questions.stem: Which additional biliary territory should the HPB team target next for {patientName}?

exhibit.caption: Constructed current duct-drainage map

Ducts are decompressed.
No stent enters this sector.
Dilation is unchanged; no new adjacent collection.
The sector filled with contrast during the prior ERCP but received no stent.
Ducts have enlarged and contain dependent debris; new small adjacent fluid collections are present.

answerChoices.label: Right posterior sectoral ducts
answerChoices.rationale: New infection findings localize to an undrained obstructed sector. Its planned removal does not remove the current need for source control.

answerChoices.label: Left hepatic duct system
answerChoices.rationale: The left drain remains functional and its ducts are decompressed. Repeating treatment there does not address the newly abnormal undrained territory.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The left drain remains functional and its ducts are decompressed. Repeating treatment there does not address the newly abnormal undrained territory.

answerChoices.label: Right anterior sectoral ducts
answerChoices.rationale: This is undrained but does not show the new inflammatory collection pattern represented in the posterior sector.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is undrained but does not show the new inflammatory collection pattern represented in the posterior sector.

questions.explanation: First determine whether the existing remnant drainage is functioning. Then localize the current infection to the contrast-filled but undrained posterior sector. Cholangitis in an obstructed residual territory can require added drainage even when that territory is planned for later resection. This does not prescribe an ERCP-versus-percutaneous access route.

questions.stem: Which treatment course should the HPB team prefer for {patientName} from this map?

exhibit.caption: Constructed MRCP and ERCP treatment map
cells: A short common hepatic duct narrowing is present above the cystic-duct insertion.
The upper edge of the narrowing is 4 mm below the right-left hepatic confluence.
Both main hepatic branches remain patent.
A guidewire passes the narrowing and can enter either hepatic branch.

answerChoices.label: ERCP placement of multiple plastic stents
answerChoices.rationale: The traversable postoperative stricture lies very close to the confluence, favoring the guideline-supported plastic strategy rather than assuming a covered metal stent will suit the available proximal cuff.

answerChoices.label: ERCP placement of a fully covered metal stent
answerChoices.rationale: This is a genuine benign-stricture strategy, but the available proximal cuff is much shorter than the guideline’s more-than-2-cm distal location for the usual postcholecystectomy alternative.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a genuine benign-stricture strategy, but the available proximal cuff is much shorter than the guideline’s more-than-2-cm distal location for the usual postcholecystectomy alternative.

answerChoices.label: Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Reconstruction is an established option for major or refractory injury, but current wire access and branch patency support an endoscopic course before that escalation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Reconstruction is an established option for major or refractory injury, but current wire access and branch patency support an endoscopic course before that escalation.

questions.explanation: Benign disease is the supplied specialist working diagnosis; the score concerns treatment anatomy. The short cuff below the confluence and preserved traversability favor multiple plastic stents among the offered courses. Covered metal stents remain valid for selected anatomy or circumstances; plastic superiority for every benign stricture is not taught.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous image-guided catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The localized accessible pocket can be drained directly. The patient has neither diffuse contamination nor an absent access window requiring operative drainage.

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic washout with drain placement
answerChoices.rationale: This is a real source-control alternative, but a contained pocket with a safe percutaneous route and stable physiology supports a less invasive initial approach.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided transluminal collection drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Expert endoscopic collection drainage is possible in selected cases, but the available percutaneous route is the established initial approach for this postoperative biloma.

nodes.explanation: First identify a localized extrabiliary pocket, then assess the available drainage path and current physiology. Those findings favor percutaneous catheter drainage as the initial source-control procedure. Operative washout addresses diffuse or inadequately controlled contamination. Endoscopic biliary diversion and drainage of a collection are different procedures.

An anterior percutaneous path enters the pocket without crossing bowel or pleura.
Stable blood pressure; tenderness remains confined to the right upper quadrant, without rigidity.

nodes.stem: Which interim drainage procedure should the consulting HPB team arrange for {patientName} before definitive repair?

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The septic proximal ducts remain obstructed despite collection drainage, and the retrograde route cannot traverse the injury. Transhepatic drainage accesses the proximal system.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: This assumes an accessible path into the obstructed proximal ducts that the attributed injection and wire attempt did not establish.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous exchange of the collection catheter
answerChoices.rationale: The collection is already collapsed; changing its catheter does not decompress the dilated proximal duct system.

nodes.explanation: The studies distinguish a controlled extrabiliary cavity from an obstructed proximal duct system. Infection persists while the papillary route cannot reach that system. Transhepatic biliary drainage is a supported interim decompression option under HPB management; no repair date or universal reconstruction is selected.

nodes.stem: Which next management plan best fits {patientName}’s completed resection and current records?

answerChoices.label: Cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented invasive carcinoma remains superficial to adequately sampled muscle, with complete removal and clear margins. Those findings do not establish a need for radical completion surgery.

answerChoices.label: Completion liver-bed resection with portal lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: This can address a deeper localized primary, but the adequately represented muscle and deeper wall here are uninvolved.

answerChoices.label: Completion extrahepatic duct resection with reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The specimen does not demonstrate residual carcinoma at the duct margin or adjacent duct wall.

nodes.explanation: The tissue must be represented before its uninvolved status is applied. Here the gross lesion is submitted, muscle beneath it is present and uninvolved, the invasive glands remain in lamina propria, and margins are clear. That supports cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy rather than completion radical resection.

nodes.stem: Which next oncologic management plan should the HPB team discuss for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Completion liver-bed resection with regional lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Perimuscular invasion supports completion oncologic surgery despite no visible residual mass; the clear duct margin does not create an indication for duct removal.

answerChoices.label: Cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A clear margin and negative CT do not make perimuscular invasion equivalent to completely removed lamina-propria-limited disease.

answerChoices.label: Completion extrahepatic duct resection with reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: This directs resection to an uninvolved duct rather than the gallbladder bed and regional nodes.

nodes.explanation: A negative staging scan does not erase the microscopic depth of invasion. For this fit patient with localized perimuscular disease, completion liver-bed and regional nodal surgery is supported. The current record does not identify residual extrahepatic duct disease.

nodes.stem: Which additional clearance procedure should the HPB team discuss for {patientName} from this specimen map?

answerChoices.label: Segmental extrahepatic duct resection with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The malignant focus is in remaining common-duct wall beyond the tumor-free cystic stump. Duct excision with reconstruction addresses that site between clear sampled division edges.

answerChoices.label: Further excision of the remaining cystic-duct stump
answerChoices.rationale: This does not remove the separately represented malignant common hepatic duct wall; the stump itself is negative.

answerChoices.label: Further resection of the gallbladder liver bed
answerChoices.rationale: This targets the wrong remaining specimen: the liver-bed margin is clear, while another oriented wall specimen contains tumor.

nodes.explanation: A negative cut edge on the removed gallbladder is not the same specimen as the remaining common hepatic duct wall sampled at completion surgery. The new map places carcinoma beyond the negative cystic stump, in a duct-wall segment bounded by clear sampled division edges. The offered clearance procedure must remove that segment rather than repeat excision of negative stump or liver-bed tissue.

nodes.stem: Which long-term biliary plan should the HPB team discuss with {patientName} after recovery?

answerChoices.label: Completion cyst excision with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The old operation drained the cyst rather than removing it. A patent opening and symptom improvement do not remove the retained abnormal duct epithelium.

answerChoices.label: Surveillance after the previous cyst operation
answerChoices.rationale: The label previous surgery does not establish excision; the record and MRCP show retained cyst tissue that still needs definitive-treatment assessment.

answerChoices.label: Revision of the cyst-duodenal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: A drainage revision may address a narrowed opening but leaves cyst epithelium in place; the current opening is patent.

nodes.explanation: Interpret what the childhood operation actually removed. It created drainage but left the cyst wall, and MRCP confirms that the abnormal duct remains. Relief of obstruction is therefore not equivalent to definitive cyst treatment. Completion excision and reconstruction warrants HPB discussion after recovery, with exact operative extent and later surveillance individualized.

The opening is patent, with no filling defect or anastomotic narrowing.

nodes.stem: Which additional biliary territory should the HPB team target next for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Right posterior sectoral ducts
answerChoices.rationale: New infection findings localize to an undrained obstructed sector. Its planned removal does not remove the current need for source control.

answerChoices.label: Left hepatic duct system
answerChoices.rationale: The left drain remains functional and its ducts are decompressed. Repeating treatment there does not address the newly abnormal undrained territory.

answerChoices.label: Right anterior sectoral ducts
answerChoices.rationale: This is undrained but does not show the new inflammatory collection pattern represented in the posterior sector.

nodes.explanation: First determine whether the existing remnant drainage is functioning. Then localize the current infection to the contrast-filled but undrained posterior sector. Cholangitis in an obstructed residual territory can require added drainage even when that territory is planned for later resection. This does not prescribe an ERCP-versus-percutaneous access route.

nodes.stem: Which treatment course should the HPB team prefer for {patientName} from this map?

answerChoices.label: ERCP placement of multiple plastic stents
answerChoices.rationale: The traversable postoperative stricture lies very close to the confluence, favoring the guideline-supported plastic strategy rather than assuming a covered metal stent will suit the available proximal cuff.

answerChoices.label: ERCP placement of a fully covered metal stent
answerChoices.rationale: This is a genuine benign-stricture strategy, but the available proximal cuff is much shorter than the guideline’s more-than-2-cm distal location for the usual postcholecystectomy alternative.

answerChoices.label: Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Reconstruction is an established option for major or refractory injury, but current wire access and branch patency support an endoscopic course before that escalation.

nodes.explanation: Benign disease is the supplied specialist working diagnosis; the score concerns treatment anatomy. The short cuff below the confluence and preserved traversability favor multiple plastic stents among the offered courses. Covered metal stents remain valid for selected anatomy or circumstances; plastic superiority for every benign stricture is not taught.

answerChoices.label: ERCP brushings with intraductal forceps biopsies
answerChoices.rationale: Intraductal sampling can assess the hilar stricture without a transperitoneal primary-lesion needle track.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided needle biopsy of the hilar primary
answerChoices.rationale: This can create a primary-lesion track outside the duct and risk compromising curative options.

decisionNodes.stem: Which interim drainage procedure should the consulting HPB team arrange for {patientName} before definitive repair?

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The septic proximal ducts remain obstructed despite collection drainage, and the retrograde route cannot traverse the injury. Transhepatic drainage accesses the proximal system.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: This assumes an accessible path into the obstructed proximal ducts that the attributed injection and wire attempt did not establish.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous exchange of the collection catheter
answerChoices.rationale: The collection is already collapsed; changing its catheter does not decompress the dilated proximal duct system.

decisionNodes.explanation: The studies distinguish a controlled extrabiliary cavity from an obstructed proximal duct system. Infection persists while the papillary route cannot reach that system. Transhepatic biliary drainage is a supported interim decompression option under HPB management; no repair date or universal reconstruction is selected.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next management plan best fits {patientName}’s completed resection and current records?

answerChoices.label: Cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented invasive carcinoma remains superficial to adequately sampled muscle, with complete removal and clear margins. Those findings do not establish a need for radical completion surgery.

answerChoices.label: Completion liver-bed resection with portal lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: This can address a deeper localized primary, but the adequately represented muscle and deeper wall here are uninvolved.

answerChoices.label: Completion extrahepatic duct resection with reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The specimen does not demonstrate residual carcinoma at the duct margin or adjacent duct wall.

That supports cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy rather than completion radical resection.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next oncologic management plan should the HPB team discuss for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Completion liver-bed resection with regional lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Perimuscular invasion supports completion oncologic surgery despite no visible residual mass; the clear duct margin does not create an indication for duct removal.

answerChoices.label: Cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A clear margin and negative CT do not make perimuscular invasion equivalent to completely removed lamina-propria-limited disease.

answerChoices.label: Completion extrahepatic duct resection with reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: This directs resection to an uninvolved duct rather than the gallbladder bed and regional nodes.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional clearance procedure should the HPB team discuss for {patientName} from this specimen map?

answerChoices.label: Segmental extrahepatic duct resection with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The malignant focus is in remaining common-duct wall beyond the tumor-free cystic stump. Duct excision with reconstruction addresses that site between clear sampled division edges.

answerChoices.label: Further excision of the remaining cystic-duct stump
answerChoices.rationale: This does not remove the separately represented malignant common hepatic duct wall; the stump itself is negative.

answerChoices.label: Further resection of the gallbladder liver bed
answerChoices.rationale: This targets the wrong remaining specimen: the liver-bed margin is clear, while another oriented wall specimen contains tumor.

decisionNodes.explanation: A negative cut edge on the removed gallbladder is not the same specimen as the remaining common hepatic duct wall sampled at completion surgery. The new map places carcinoma beyond the negative cystic stump, in a duct-wall segment bounded by clear sampled division edges. The offered clearance procedure must remove that segment rather than repeat excision of negative stump or liver-bed tissue.

decisionNodes.stem: Which long-term biliary plan should the HPB team discuss with {patientName} after recovery?

answerChoices.label: Completion cyst excision with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The old operation drained the cyst rather than removing it. A patent opening and symptom improvement do not remove the retained abnormal duct epithelium.

answerChoices.label: Surveillance after the previous cyst operation
answerChoices.rationale: The label previous surgery does not establish excision; the record and MRCP show retained cyst tissue that still needs definitive-treatment assessment.

answerChoices.label: Revision of the cyst-duodenal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: A drainage revision may address a narrowed opening but leaves cyst epithelium in place; the current opening is patent.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret what the childhood operation actually removed. It created drainage but left the cyst wall, and MRCP confirms that the abnormal duct remains. Relief of obstruction is therefore not equivalent to definitive cyst treatment. Completion excision and reconstruction warrants HPB discussion after recovery, with exact operative extent and later surveillance individualized.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional biliary territory should the HPB team target next for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Right posterior sectoral ducts
answerChoices.rationale: New infection findings localize to an undrained obstructed sector. Its planned removal does not remove the current need for source control.

answerChoices.label: Left hepatic duct system
answerChoices.rationale: The left drain remains functional and its ducts are decompressed. Repeating treatment there does not address the newly abnormal undrained territory.

answerChoices.label: Right anterior sectoral ducts
answerChoices.rationale: This is undrained but does not show the new inflammatory collection pattern represented in the posterior sector.

decisionNodes.explanation: First determine whether the existing remnant drainage is functioning. Then localize the current infection to the contrast-filled but undrained posterior sector. Cholangitis in an obstructed residual territory can require added drainage even when that territory is planned for later resection. This does not prescribe an ERCP-versus-percutaneous access route.

decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment course should the HPB team prefer for {patientName} from this map?

answerChoices.label: ERCP placement of multiple plastic stents
answerChoices.rationale: The traversable postoperative stricture lies very close to the confluence, favoring the guideline-supported plastic strategy rather than assuming a covered metal stent will suit the available proximal cuff.

answerChoices.label: ERCP placement of a fully covered metal stent
answerChoices.rationale: This is a genuine benign-stricture strategy, but the available proximal cuff is much shorter than the guideline’s more-than-2-cm distal location for the usual postcholecystectomy alternative.

answerChoices.label: Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Reconstruction is an established option for major or refractory injury, but current wire access and branch patency support an endoscopic course before that escalation.

decisionNodes.explanation: Benign disease is the supplied specialist working diagnosis; the score concerns treatment anatomy. The short cuff below the confluence and preserved traversability favor multiple plastic stents among the offered courses. Covered metal stents remain valid for selected anatomy or circumstances; plastic superiority for every benign stricture is not taught.
